title: # Rabbi Aryeh Levin
content:
Rabbi Aryeh Levin

This text surveys the life and character of Rabbi Aryeh Levin, sketching a mosaic that combines profound Torah scholarship with boundless social kindness. The survey opens with his roots in Lithuania and the formative encounter with Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, and continues with a description of his unique activity as **"the Prisoners' Rabbi"** who served as a spiritual support for underground fighters and accompanied those condemned to death in their final moments. Alongside his national activity, the text emphasizes the exceptional moral sensitivity he displayed toward marginalized groups, such as leprosy patients at the Hansen Hospital, and his educational method based on love and drawing hearts near. The aim of the article is to present how Levin's personality bridged gaps in Israeli society, and made him a symbol of "radical love of Israel" that fuses halakhic precision with pure humaneness.

The Figure of the Jerusalem Tzaddik: The Torah, Moral and National Work of Rabbi Aryeh Levin

The historiography of the Jewish Yishuv in the Land of Israel in the twentieth century is studded with leadership figures, but few are the individuals who merited such broad consensus and such deep affection among all strata of the people as Rabbi Aryeh Levin (1885–1969). His figure, known by the epithets "the Prisoners' Rabbi," "Father of the Prisoners," and "the Jerusalem Tzaddik," cannot be encapsulated in dry biographical terms alone.[1, 2] This is a personality that fused within itself the meticulous Lithuanian learnedness, the spiritual openness of the Torah of the Land of Israel in the style of Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, and the absolute moral self-sacrifice toward the weak and downtrodden.[3, 4] Analysis of his work and Torah teaching requires a dive into the depth of the formative stations in his life, from the small towns in White Russia to the besieged alleyways of Jerusalem during the British Mandate period and the War of Independence.

The Roots in Lithuania and Formation of Torah Identity

Rabbi Aryeh Levin was born on the sixth of Nisan 5645 (March 22, 1885) in the town of Orla, near Białystok, within the "Pale of Settlement" of the Jewish population of the Russian Empire.[1, 5] His father, Benjamin Beinush, was a simple forester, and his mother Ettel managed a household characterized by material poverty but spiritual wealth.[2, 5] The severe economic distress in his parents' home forced him to wander between yeshivot at a very young age, a path that was common among "prodigies" at that time.[3]

The educational path of the young Rabbi Levin is a map of the Lithuanian yeshiva world at its zenith. He studied in Slutsk, in Slonim, in Brisk and in Pinsk, and each station added another layer to his method of study.[5] One of the most significant stations was at the yeshiva of Holosk, where he merited to study with Rabbi Baruch Dov Leibowitz, author of the *Birkat Shmuel*, who was considered one of the greatest scholars of his generation.[5] The influence of Rabbi Baruch Dov is evident in the halakhic precision and intellectual clarity that characterize Rabbi Levin's later writings.

His great aspiration was to be accepted to the Volozhin Yeshiva, "the mother of yeshivot." Initially he was rejected due to his young age, but after a year of stubborn perseverance he was accepted to study with Rabbi Raphael Shapira.[2, 5] In Volozhin he absorbed the tradition of deep learning and the ideal of "diligence" – continuous Torah study day and night, an ideal that accompanied him all his life.[2]

The Encounter with the Land of Israel and Rabbi Kook: A Consciousness Revolution

In the year 5665 (1905), at the age of 19, Rabbi Aryeh Levin decided to immigrate to the Land of Israel.[3] His arrival at the port of Jaffa was a turning point not only in his personal life, but in the shaping of his rabbinic model. In Jaffa he met for the first time Rabbi Abraham Isaac HaCohen Kook, who was then rabbi of the city and the agricultural settlements.[3] The encounter between the two was not merely technical; it represented a connection between the old Lithuanian learnedness and the "lights" of the revival of the Land of Israel.

Rabbi Levin described in his memoirs how Rabbi Kook received him with a cheerful countenance and conversed with him in words of Torah.[6] A formative event during that period occurred during a walking tour by the two in the fields of Jaffa after the Minḥah prayer. Rabbi Levin plucked a flower or plant absent-mindedly, and Rabbi Kook remarked to him gently that from time immemorial he had refrained from plucking plants without need, since "every plant sings a song."[6] This saying, taken from the world of Kabbalah and Hasidism, penetrated deeply into Rabbi Levin's soul and became the moral foundation of his attitude toward every living creature.

The connection with Rabbi Kook deepened over the years. Rabbi Kook was the one who identified in Rabbi Levin the exceptional qualities suitable for the role of "Prisoners' Rabbi," and he was the one who sent him on this mission in the year 5691 (1931), out of an understanding that only a person of such spiritual stature could bridge the gaps between the ḥaredi world and the world of the young fighters in the underground movements.[3, 7]

The Leader Within the Home: Family and Modesty

Shortly after his arrival in Jerusalem, on the eighth of Tammuz 5665, Rabbi Aryeh married Tziporah Hannah Shapira, daughter of Rabbi David Shapira of Kovno.[1, 5] This marriage brought him into the heart of the Torah elite of Jerusalem; his father-in-law was the son of Rabbi Ḥaim Yaakov Shapira and brother-in-law of Rabbi Tzvi Pesaḥ Frank, Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem.[2, 5]

The family life of Rabbi Levin was characterized by extreme material poverty but great spiritual happiness. The couple lived in a small one-room apartment in the "Mishkenot" neighborhood (Har Gerizim Street, whose name was later changed to Rabbi Aryeh Levin Street).[5, 8] During the First World War the family endured severe years of famine, during which two of their daughters died due to lack of food and medicine.[5] Despite these tragedies, Rabbi Levin's home remained open to all in need. He was accustomed to distribute the little food he had with his neighbors, and in the War of Liberation, when Jerusalem was under siege, he hastened to distribute food products that Leḥi members brought him among the needy families in his vicinity.[1]

The most famous story about his married life is his visit to the doctor with his wife. The rabbi turned to the doctor and said: "My wife's leg hurts us."[9] This sentence became a symbol of his ability to identify completely with the other, to the point of eliminating the barrier between another's pain and his own pain. The Rebbetzin herself testified that their life was characterized by the quality of self-abnegation and deep connection, "like a pair of doves."[9]

His Educational Doctrine at "Etz Ḥaim": A Pedagogy of Love

Beginning in the year 5677 (1917) Rabbi Aryeh Levin served as mashgiaḥ in the Talmud Torah and in Yeshivat "Etz Ḥaim" in Jerusalem.[5, 10] The role of mashgiaḥ in the yeshiva world of that time was usually associated with enforcing discipline and preaching sharp rebuke. However, Rabbi Levin effected a quiet revolution in this role. He chose the path of "pleasant ways," out of a belief that the only way to shape a child's soul is through warmth and love.[11]

He saw in children the "dust and stones" of the Land of Israel in the sense of "for Your servants hold her stones dear, and cherish her dust."[12] For him, caressing a child's face was a religious commandment no less than studying a page of Gemara. He believed that "good character traits are acquired through good deeds," and that the educator must be a living example of one who possesses such traits.[3] His students at "Etz Ḥaim" remember him as one who did not give up on any child, even on those who were defined as "difficult" or "rebellious," and always found the way to soften their hearts with pleasant speech and a cheerful countenance.[11]

The Prisoners' Rabbi: National Mission and Religious Devotion

The title "Prisoners' Rabbi" or "Father of the Prisoners" is not merely an honorific title, but an accurate description of a life's work that lasted some 25 years.[2, 5] It all began in the year 1931 (5691), when the British Mandate authorities sought a rabbi who would visit the Jewish prisoners in the jails.[3] Rabbi Kook directed them to Rabbi Levin, explaining that this difficult mission required a person of spiritual fortitude and exceptional character traits.[7]

Every Sabbath and holiday, regardless of weather, security situation, or days of curfew, Rabbi Levin would walk on foot from his home in the Mishkenot neighborhood to the Central Prison in Jerusalem (at the "Russian Compound") or to Acre.[5, 13] He refused to use vehicular transport on the Sabbath, despite the great distance and the danger
humility, out of devotion to halakha and a desire to show the prisoners his personal commitment to them.[10, 13]

The prisoners, among them members of the Etzel and Lehi underground movements, saw him as a father figure. Rabbi Levin did not engage in politics; he saw in every Jewish prisoner a "holy spark" that needed encouragement.[8] He would memorize detailed greetings from the prisoners and deliver them to their families after the Sabbath ended, as he made his rounds on foot through Jerusalem on his weary legs.[3] For the prisoners, the visit of "Rabbi Aryeh" was the only ray of light within the darkness of the cell.[1]

Treatment of Those Condemned to the Gallows

The pinnacle of his activity in the prison was accompanying those condemned to death, "those who ascended the gallows." Rabbi Levin established a deep spiritual connection with fighters such as Moshe Barazani and Meir Feinstein.[7, 14] He described tearfully how he laid tefillin on them for the last time before their execution, and how they wept that they would not merit to fulfill this commandment again.[14] Even though there were among them those who did not observe Torah and commandments in their daily lives, before Rabbi Levin they felt comfortable revealing their hidden faith.

Despite being a Haredi rabbi, he earned unprecedented admiration from the secular underground fighters. They saw him as "their" rabbi, the one who understood their self-sacrifice for national redemption.[1, 8] Shortly before his death in 1969, he was awarded the "State Warriors Medal" for this work, a decoration he accepted with his characteristic modesty.[5, 10]

"Father of the Lepers": Kindness in the Most Ostracized Place

One of the most moving chapters in the life of Rabbi Aryeh Levin is his volunteer work at the Hansen Hospital for lepers in the Talbiyeh neighborhood of Jerusalem.[15] Leprosy in those days was considered not only a severe physical disease but a terrible social stigma. The patients were isolated from society, and many of them were abandoned by their families who feared contagion.[15]

Rabbi Levin arrived at the place after hearing a weeping mother who told him that her son was hospitalized in the hospital and she dared not visit him.[15, 16] Without hesitation, the rabbi put his life at risk and began to visit the hospital regularly.[16] He discovered there additional Jewish patients living in stark loneliness. The rabbi decided to take them under his care; he visited them weekly, brought them kosher food that his wife cooked, and saw to all their spiritual needs.[15]

Every Rosh Hashanah, he would come to the hospital with his sons to blow the shofar for the patients.[15] This act embodied the essence of his moral teaching: true kindness is not performed in glittering places, but specifically in places that no one wants to look at. The patients testified that Rabbi Levin was the first person who treated them as equal human beings, and not as "lepers" to be kept at a distance.[5, 16]

The Goral HaGra and Identification of the Lamed Heh Casualties: Between Mysticism and Nationalism

After the War of Independence, the young State of Israel faced a difficult national tragedy. Twelve of the 35 fighters of the Lamed Heh convoy who fell on their way to Gush Etzion were not identified with certainty when their bodies were transferred for permanent burial in Jerusalem.[2, 17] The military rabbinate and the bereaved families faced a dead end.[17]

At this stage, in consultation with the rabbi of Jerusalem, Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank, it was decided to conduct the "Goral HaGra" – an ancient Jewish procedure attributed to the Vilna Gaon, designed to receive answers to fateful questions through random opening of a Tanakh.[18, 19] The task was assigned to Rabbi Aryeh Levin, who was perceived as the most authorized and holy figure to perform the ceremony.[19]

The ceremony was held in the rabbi's home in the presence of representatives of the bereaved families (among them Reuven Mass and Yitzhak Dov HaKohen Persitz).[19] The rabbi used an ancient Tanakh printed in Amsterdam in 1651.[19] The results were astonishing and left an indelible impression on those present.

The identifications were accepted without objection by the families and the IDF, and the fallen were brought to burial under their names on Mount Herzl.[19] This event demonstrates how Rabbi Levin served as a connecting link between the world of ancient Jewish tradition and the acute needs of the nascent Israeli society, while providing spiritual solace to bereaved families from across the spectrum.[19]

His Torah Teaching in Writing and Deed

Despite his public persona focusing on acts of kindness, Rabbi Aryeh Levin was a distinguished Torah scholar with exceptional writing and analytical ability. His most important Torah work is "Mishnat Aryeh," a systematic and comprehensive commentary on the Mishnayot.[2, 20] The manuscript of this work, spanning two thick notebooks and over a thousand pages, was discovered only after his death.[20]

In "Mishnat Aryeh," Rabbi Levin demonstrates enormous expertise in Rishonim and Aḥaronim, as he distills the plain meaning of the Mishnah in light of the Talmud. The work was published by "The Committee for Publishing the Writings of Rabbi Aryeh Levin" under the editorship of Rabbi Yechiel Sternberg, and constitutes an invaluable asset in the yeshiva world.[20, 21, 22]

In addition, Rabbi Levin saw great importance in preserving the legacy of his teachers and close associates. He wrote the biography of his father-in-law, the kabbalist Rabbi Shlomo Elyashiv, author of "Leshem Shevo Ve-Aḥlamah."[2, 23] His relationship with the "Leshem" was especially deep; after Rabbi Elyashiv's aliyah to the Land of Israel, Rabbi Levin became his foremost student and assisted him greatly in his personal and public affairs.[5, 23]

Additional books that compile his moral teachings and stories are:

"Rabbi Aryeh Would Say" – Tractate Avot with teachings heard from his mouth, edited by Simcha Raz.[2]

"He Was a Righteous Man" – a detailed and inspiring biography written by Simcha Raz, which became one of the most influential books on the "tzaddik's" persona in Israeli culture.[8]

Yeshivat "Beit Aryeh"

With the establishment of the State, Rabbi Levin founded Yeshivat "Beit Aryeh" in the courtyard of his home in Jerusalem.[5, 10] He chose to place at the head of the yeshiva his son-in-law, Rabbi Eliezer Platzinsky, who was the grandson of the "Alter of Slabodka."[10] The yeshiva was established not as a center of power and authority, but as a hothouse for raising Torah scholars in the spirit of Rabbi Levin's character traits and kindness.[5] The place continues to operate to this day and serves as a pilgrimage site for people seeking to experience the atmosphere of old Jerusalem.[5, 8]

Ethics and Interpersonal Relations: The Practice of Holiness

In Rabbi Levin's eyes, the true measure of fear of Heaven was not only in Torah study, but in one's treatment of the simplest person. He made a point of greeting the street cleaners of Jerusalem with "good morning" on his way to the vatikin prayer service (according to the custom of the Vilna Gaon).[13] When asked why he devoted such attention to them, he replied that he appreciated people who work hard while others sleep, so that Jerusalem would be clean and dignified.[13]

He actively pursued peace. It is told that once he heard a neighbor reporting a thief breaking into a kiosk. The rabbi hurried to the place, and instead of shouting or summoning help, he turned to the thief in a fatherly whisper: "My son, perhaps you forgot what is written in the Torah: 'You shall not steal'?".[13] The thief, surprised by the non-judgmental and respectful approach, put down the stolen goods and left the place in shame.

Spiritual Legacy and Summary

Rabbi Aryeh Levin passed away on the eve of Shabbat HaGadol, 9 Sivan 5729 (May 26, 1969), and was buried in the Sanhedriya cemetery next to his wife's grave.[1, 10] His death marked the end of an era in which rabbinic figures could serve as a living bridge between such distant extremes of Israeli society.

Rabbi Levin's Torah and moral teaching can be summed up in the concept of "radical love of Israel." This was not a theoretical love, but a love that found expression in every step taken in the alleyways of Jerusalem, in every letter he wrote to a prisoner and in every caress he gave to an orphaned child.[8, 24] He proved that meticulous observance of Torah commandments does not contradict deep social sensitivity, but on the contrary – it is its engine.

His spiritual testament, engraved on his tombstone, asks all who come to his grave to refrain from controversy, to love one another, and to recite the formula of "Ani Ma'amin" dealing with the resurrection of the dead.[3, 5] The figure of Rabbi Levin continues to shine even today, in
through his books, the yeshiva he established, and especially through countless stories of his acts of kindness, which constitute a beacon of refined Jewish humanitarianism in the heart of the turbulent history of the Jewish people in the modern era.[5, 8]

From a historical perspective, Rabbi Aryeh Levin was not merely a "rabbi" in the institutional sense of the word, but a "tzaddik" in the most ancient and profound sense—a person whose entire being was consecrated to the collective, and who in his remarkable personality succeeded in transforming the suffering of others into prayer and their distress into an act of redemption.[8, 19]
